Bacterial Meningitis

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Fever with headache, a stiff neck or altered mental status in a child, or only lethargy, irritability, poor feeding and a bulging fontanelle in an infant: suspect bacterial meningitis; a supple neck does not exclude it under 12 months.
  • Blood cultures, then the lumbar puncture, then IV antibiotics; when a red flag for raised pressure (step 4) or shock delays the tap, cultures and antibiotics come first and the CT after.
  • The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) decides: neutrophils with low glucose is bacterial, lymphocytes with normal glucose viral. Treat with ampicillin plus cefotaxime under 1 month, vancomycin plus ceftriaxone after, and dexamethasone with the first dose for Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) or pneumococcus.
What it is

Bacterial infection of the leptomeninges (pia and arachnoid) and the subarachnoid space; lethal untreated, so even a small chance of it earns a lumbar puncture.

Bug

Under 1 month: group B Streptococcus (GBS), then Escherichia coli (K1 capsule strains), then Listeria monocytogenes; mnemonic newborn GEL (GBS, E. coli, Listeria).

Children: Streptococcus pneumoniae. Adolescents: Neisseria meningitidis, a gram-negative diplococcus. Unvaccinated child: Hib, the only H. influenzae capsular type that causes meningitis.

Adults: S. pneumoniae; in older adults, also Listeria and gram-negative rods; Listeria also in pregnancy or immunocompromise.

Viral (aseptic) meningitis: enteroviruses, coxsackievirus and echovirus, are the most common cause of meningitis at every age.

Spread

Most often respiratory droplets and throat secretions; the organism most commonly reaches the meninges through the blood.

Meningococcus: carriage peaks in adolescents and young adults; dormitories, military recruits; asplenia, terminal complement deficiency (C5 to C9) or eculizumab.

Pneumococcus and Hib: asplenia or sickle cell disease, a nearby sinus or ear infection or a CSF leak, and missed conjugate vaccines (given from 2 months).

Listeria: contaminated food, the placenta or the birth canal. Ventricular shunt or neurosurgery: S. epidermidis and gram-negative rods.

Chain

Organism colonizes the nose and throat

reaches the subarachnoid space through the blood

bacterial lysis releases cytokines that open the blood-brain barrier

neutrophils flood the CSF; cerebral edema raises intracranial pressure

herniation; scarred arachnoid granulations that may cause hydrocephalus; hearing loss and seizures as later sequelae

Insights

Antibiotics sterilize the CSF, so the tap comes first when it can be done at once; when it cannot, blood cultures drawn before the first dose still name the organism.

Dexamethasone protects the cochlea: it blunts the inflammation that injures cranial nerve VIII, so it goes in before or with the first antibiotic dose.

2Urgent risks
Urgent findings
FindingAction
Papilledema, a focal deficit, a seizure or obtundationBlood cultures and antibiotics now; CT before any tap (step 4).
Hypotension or shock (cardiorespiratory compromise, most often in young infants)Treat the shock, draw blood cultures and give antibiotics; the tap waits.
Spreading nonblanching petechiae or purpuraMeningococcemia: antibiotics without delay; check platelets and fibrinogen, typically low in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
3Differential
Fever with meningeal signs or a lethargic infant
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Bacterial meningitisNeutrophils, low glucose, high protein, high opening pressure; the Gram stain may show the organism.Empiric antibiotics by age (step 7).
Viral (aseptic) meningitisLate summer or fall in the United States; lymphocytes, normal glucose, normal or raised protein.CSF enterovirus polymerase chain reaction (PCR); supportive care.
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitisAltered mental status, seizures, aphasia or focal signs; lymphocytes with red cells; in a newborn, lethargy may be the only sign.Start IV acyclovir now; send a CSF HSV PCR to confirm.
MeningococcemiaFever and myalgia, then nonblanching petechiae and purpura that spread rapidly, often on the legs; shock and DIC can follow.Blood cultures and antibiotics without waiting; droplet precautions (step 8).
Lymphocytes or a mixed count, low glucose, high protein; basilar enhancement and hydrocephalus.CSF acid-fast stain, mycobacterial culture and PCR.
Cryptococcal meningitisHuman immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or other immunocompromise; lymphocytes with low glucose.Send a CSF antigen test (step 4).
A seizure with fever and no meningeal signs.No tap unless meningeal signs, or an unimmunized infant of 6-12 months; otherwise supportive care.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Young child, no red flagHerniation from the tap is rare; a routine CT adds nothingDo the lumbar puncture without a CT first.
Petechial rash on the legs with a positive Brudzinski signMeningococcal meningitis; a positive Brudzinski sign is specific, not sensitiveBlood cultures and antibiotics; droplet precautions.
Lymphocytes with red cells in the CSFHSV encephalitisIV acyclovir now; send the CSF HSV PCR.
Antibiotics given before the tapThe culture may be sterileRead the cell count and glucose; blood cultures and a PCR panel can still name the organism.
Pause point
Febrile child, stiff neck, the CT scanner busy for an hour Offered as wait for the CT and the tap or antibiotics only after the tap Will the tap be delayed? → Blood cultures and antibiotics now; scan and tap afterward
Newborn with seizures and lethargy; CSF lymphocytes and red cells Offered as group B Streptococcus or E. coli Neutrophils or lymphocytes, and are there red cells? → HSV encephalitis: IV acyclovir
Vaccinated household contact of a child with meningococcal meningitis Offered as no prophylaxis, since vaccinated or a vaccine booster instead Does vaccination remove the need for prophylaxis? → Rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone, whatever the vaccine status
5Diagnostic criteria
CSF patterns
DiagnosisCellsGlucoseProtein
BacterialNeutrophil-predominant; white cells often over 1,000/mm³LowHigh MSD (Merck Sharp and Dohme) Manual: protein over 100 mg/dL; glucose under 40 mg/dL, often under 10, with a CSF to blood glucose ratio typically under 0.33.
ViralLymphocytes; neutrophils may be mixed in during the first 24 to 48 hoursNormalNormal or raised
HSV encephalitisLymphocytes with red cellsNormal or mildly lowMildly raised
TuberculousLymphocytes, often mixed with neutrophilsLowHigh
Fungal (cryptococcal)LymphocytesLowHigh

Opening pressure is raised in bacterial, tuberculous and fungal meningitis and normal or raised in viral meningitis. Some neonates with meningitis have normal counts, so the culture decides.

6Severity
What makes it severe
FindingMeaning
Obtundation or coma; hypertension, bradycardia and slow breathing (Cushing triad); papilledemaRaised intracranial pressure; herniation is the commonest cause of death in the acute stages
Purpura with shock, low platelets and low fibrinogenMeningococcemia with DIC
Shock that deepens after purpuraWaterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: bilateral adrenal hemorrhage; the lost cortisol worsens the hypotension
Low sodiumSyndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
Neonate not improving on antibioticsVentriculitis or brain abscess: repeat the tap and image the brain
7Treatment
1

NeonateUnder 1 month

IV ampicillin plus cefotaxime, with or without gentamicin; cefotaxime, not ceftriaxone, because ceftriaxone raises bilirubin. Ampicillin covers Listeria; cefotaxime enters the central nervous system better than gentamicin.

2

Child or adultOver 1 month

IV vancomycin plus ceftriaxone: ceftriaxone covers meningococcus and other gram-negatives; vancomycin is added for cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus. In practice: once the organism and its susceptibilities are known, therapy narrows and vancomycin may stop.

3

Listeria riskOver 50, pregnancy or immunocompromise

Add IV ampicillin for Listeria.

4

AdjunctSuspected Hib or pneumococcal meningitis after 6 weeks of age

IV dexamethasone just before or with the first antibiotic dose, every 6 hours for 4 days, to cut hearing loss. In adults it is best established for pneumococcal meningitis; high-dose steroids worsen meningococcal shock without meningitis.

5

HSV possibleEncephalitis signs or lymphocytes with red cells

Add IV acyclovir until HSV is ruled out.

6

Shunt or neurosurgeryVentricular shunt or recent neurosurgery

Vancomycin plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime.

8Follow-up
Contacts, isolation and aftercare
WhenDo
Meningococcal diseaseClose contacts (household, child care in the prior 7 days, anyone exposed to oral secretions): rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone, whatever their vaccine status, ideally within 24 hours. For young children, rifampin by mouth or ceftriaxone by injection is the preferred choice; ciprofloxacin suits older contacts.
Hib meningitisRifampin for the household when it includes an incompletely immunized child under 4 or an infant under 12 months without the primary series.
Pneumococcus or other bacteriaNo prophylaxis for contacts.
Health care workersProphylaxis only after managing the airway or direct exposure to respiratory secretions.
AdmissionDroplet precautions for meningococcus and Hib until 24 hours of effective antibiotics.
Every survivorAudiologic testing and developmental follow-up: hearing loss is the most common sequela in children; sensorineural loss is most common after pneumococcal meningitis.
Recurrent or unusual Neisseria infectionCH50 (total hemolytic complement) after recovery, for a terminal complement deficiency: the membrane attack complex is the main defense against Neisseria.
PreventionWhere given routinely, Hib and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, both from 2 months, make meningitis from these organisms rare; the schedule is owned by
Practice
  1. 22 yo M with fever and neck stiffness; CSF 3,000 neutrophils, glucose 25, protein 180 → Bacterial meningitis → dexamethasone with ceftriaxone and vancomycin
  2. 22 yo M with CSF 200 lymphocytes, normal glucose and mildly raised protein → Viral meningitis
  3. 35 yo M with HIV; CSF lymphocytes, very low glucose, high protein, basilar involvement → Tuberculous meningitis
  4. 22 yo M with suspected meningitis and papilledema on fundoscopy → CT head before lumbar puncture
  5. 22 yo M with suspected bacterial meningitis and a delayed CT scanner → Blood cultures and antibiotics before imaging
  6. 68 yo M with bacterial meningitis; what coverage must be added → Ampicillin for Listeria
  7. 8 yo M in summer, headache, fever, stiff neck, CSF with 200 WBCs and 85% lymphocytes, protein 60, glucose 55, Gram stain negative → Enteroviral meningitis → supportive care
  8. 5 yo F with fever and meningismus, CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein, well appearing → Supportive care and observation → viral meningitis
  9. The most common cause of aseptic meningitis in a child presenting during summer → Enterovirus → supportive care is sufficient
  10. 2 yo with fever, hypotension, lethargy and a purpuric rash on the legs; cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci → Serum fibrinogen → purpura signals disseminated intravascular coagulation
  11. When complement testing is indicated in a patient with meningococcal disease → After recovery, for recurrent or unusual-serogroup infection → terminal complement deficiency is C5 to C9, a predisposition rather than an acute study
  12. 1 year old with meningococcemia who develops large purpuric lesions and sudden vasomotor collapse and dies; the autopsy finding → Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage → Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
  13. Infant with fever, nuchal rigidity, spreading purpura and abrupt hypotension → Fulminant meningococcemia → purpura with shock; adrenal hemorrhage makes it Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
  14. 16 yo M, 8 hours of abrupt high fever and sore throat with severe diffuse leg pain, says he has never felt this terrible; pale, nonexudative pharyngitis, supple neck, mottled tender legs; rapid strep and influenza negative; complete blood count and blood culture drawn → Lumbar puncture → early meningococcal disease; no seizure, obtundation, focal deficit, papilledema or immunocompromise, so no CT first, and ceftriaxone does not wait
  15. Adolescent 10 hours into an abrupt febrile illness with severe leg pain, cold hands and feet and mottled skin, no rash yet → Meningococcemia → poor perfusion and severe myalgia arrive before the petechiae
Sequencing Order of events: blood cultures, the lumbar puncture, then antibiotics; when a red flag delays the tap, antibiotics come before the CT. Step 4 gives the CT rule and step 7 the regimen by age.
Early meningococcal disease Onset – fever, myalgia, vomiting and headache · Red flags – severe leg pain, pallor, mottling or cold hands and feet before any rash ⚠︎ · Tempo – petechiae, neck stiffness and altered mental status can follow rapidly · Workup – blood cultures and the tap (step 4), antibiotics without waiting · Complications – shock, DIC, adrenal hemorrhage (step 6) · Contacts – droplet precautions and prophylaxis (step 8)
Follow-up facts The classic triad of fever, nuchal rigidity and altered mental status appears together in only about half of patients, and often not in neonates · eculizumab blocks terminal complement and raises meningococcal risk; its vaccine rule is in .
